h1: How Many Seeds per Square Meter? Calculator + Density Table
description: Enter your garden area and crop type to instantly calculate seeds needed per m². Includes a density table for lettuce (60/m²), carrot (200/m²), tomato (10/m²), radish (110/m²) and spinach (100/m²). Free, no sign-up.
answerSnippet: Seeds needed = garden area (m²) × seed density for the crop. Key densities: carrot 200 seeds/m², radish 110 seeds/m², spinach 100 seeds/m², lettuce 60 seeds/m², tomato (seedling tray) 10 seeds/m². For a 10 m² carrot patch: 10 × 200 = 2,000 seeds. Always sow 15–20% extra to compensate for germination failures.
intro:
Knowing **how many seeds per square meter** to sow is the single most important number before you buy seed packets. Sow too few and you get bare patches; sow too many and plants compete for light and water, producing stunted, low-quality crops. This calculator gives you the answer instantly: enter your garden area and select your crop.

The formula is simple:

**Seeds needed = Area (m²) × Seed density (seeds/m²)**

Then add **15–20 % extra** to cover seeds that fail to germinate — field germination rates typically run 70–85 %, even for fresh commercial seed.

## Seed density table by crop

| Crop | Seeds/m² (sowing) | Final plants/m² | Germination rate |
|---|---|---|---|
| Carrot | 200 | 80–100 | 65–75 % |
| Radish | 110 | 80–100 | 80–90 % |
| Spinach | 100 | 60–80 | 60–70 % |
| Lettuce | 60 | 16–25 | 75–85 % |
| Tomato (tray) | 10 | 3–4 | 80–90 % |

*Reference values per USDA Cooperative Extension and RHS growing guides.*

For **tomatoes**, the density shown is for seedling trays — you sow 2 seeds per cell, thin to the strongest, then transplant at ~3–4 plants/m² in the final bed.
keyTakeaway: **Seeds needed = area (m²) × density (seeds/m²).** Key benchmarks: carrot 200/m², radish 110/m², spinach 100/m², lettuce 60/m², tomato tray 10/m². Add 15–20 % for germination failures. Example: 10 m² of carrot = 2,000 seeds ≈ one standard 5 g commercial packet.
useCases: Planning a 10 m² backyard carrot bed: 10 × 200 = 2,000 seeds, plus 15% buffer = 2,300 seeds — one standard commercial packet (typically 1,000–5,000 seeds per 5 g).
Sizing a 5 m² lettuce plot: 5 × 60 = 300 seeds, plus 20% buffer = 360 seeds, roughly one small foil packet.

Starting tomato seedlings for a 20 m² final bed: 20 × 3.5 final plants = 70 plants needed; at 85% germination, sow 83 seeds in trays — easily covered by a standard 0.2 g packet (≈ 60 seeds) plus one extra packet.
Setting up a 12-plot community garden (3 m² each): calculate seed needs per species across 36 m² total area before bulk-ordering.
Comparing seed quantity to packet weight when labels show grams instead of seed count — knowing the seeds-per-gram figure for each species.
Teaching school children practical math: compute seed requirements for a 5 m² school garden plot using multiplication and percentages.
Planning succession sowings of radish every 2 weeks in a 2 m² strip: each sowing = 2 × 110 = 220 seeds, budget for 6–8 sowings per season.
Stretching a limited gardening budget by ordering exact quantities rather than buying excess packets whose viability drops after 2–3 years of storage.
explanation:
## Cómo funciona el cálculo

La fórmula multiplica el área de siembra por la **densidad recomendada** para ese cultivo:

```
Semillas necesarias = Área (m²) × Densidad (semillas/m²)
```

Para compensar pérdidas por germinación, se aplica un margen adicional:

```
Semillas a comprar = Semillas × (1 + margen de germinación)
                   = 2,000 × 1.15 = 2,300  [zanahoria, 10 m²]
```

El margen del 15 % corresponde a una tasa de germinación real del ~87 %. Si tus semillas son viejas o las condiciones de suelo son subóptimas, usa 20–30 %.

---

## Tabla de densidades usadas en esta calculadora

| Cultivo | Semillas/m² | Por qué |
|---|---|---|
| **Zanahoria** | 200 | Semilla pequeña; se ralea a 80–100 plantas/m² con espaciado 5×2 cm |
| **Rábano** | 110 | Ciclo rápido (25–35 días); raleo final a ~80 plantas/m² con 5×5 cm |
| **Espinaca** | 100 | Se ralea a 60–80 plantas/m² con espaciado 8×10 cm |
| **Lechuga** | 60 | Variedades de cabeza: 16–25 plantas/m²; baby-leaf: hasta 80–100/m² |
| **Tomate** | 10 | Solo para bandejas de almácigo — 2 semillas por celda; trasplante final a 3–4 plantas/m² |

> **Nota sobre el tomate:** esta densidad aplica exclusivamente a semilleros. En el cantero definitivo, el tomate ocupa 0,25–0,33 m² por planta (marco 50×60 cm o 60×70 cm), por lo que sembrar directo en cama no es práctico ni rentable.

---

## Por qué la tasa de germinación es el factor crítico

Las etiquetas comerciales garantizan 80–90 % de germinación **en condiciones de laboratorio** (temperatura controlada, sustrato estéril). En un cantero exterior, los factores que reducen esa cifra son:

- **Temperatura del suelo:** la mayoría de hortalizas germina de forma óptima entre 15 °C y 25 °C. Por debajo de 10 °C, la zanahoria puede tardar 3 semanas y la tasa cae a menos del 50 %.
- **Humedad desuniforme:** el suelo que se seca entre riegos interrumpe el proceso; la semilla que ya inició la imbibición y se deshidrata no recupera viabilidad.
- **Profundidad de siembra:** sembrar demasiado profundo es la causa número 1 de fallo en semillas pequeñas. Zanahoria y lechuga no deben superar 5–6 mm de profundidad; la luz favorece su germinación.
- **Edad de la semilla:** la zanahoria pierde viabilidad con rapidez (2–3 años en buenas condiciones); el tomate y la lechuga pueden mantener >80 % hasta 4–5 años si se almacenan en frío y seco.

**Test de viabilidad casero:** coloca 10 semillas sobre papel de cocina húmedo dentro de una bolsa cerrada a temperatura ambiente (18–22 °C). Revisa a los 7–10 días. Si germinan 7, tu tasa es del 70 % y debes sembrar un 43 % más de lo calculado (`1 / 0,70 = 1,43`).

---

## De gramos a unidades: convertir el peso del sobre

Los sobres comerciales indican peso, no cantidad. Valores aproximados verificados por catálogos de semillas estándar (ISTA / catálogos europeos):

| Cultivo | Semillas/gramo | Sobre típico | Unidades aprox. |
|---|---|---|---|
| Zanahoria | 700–1,000 | 2 g | 1,400–2,000 |
| Lechuga | 700–1,000 | 1 g | 700–1,000 |
| Rábano | 80–120 | 5 g | 400–600 |
| Espinaca | 80–100 | 5 g | 400–500 |
| Tomate | 250–350 | 0,5 g | 125–175 |

Con estos datos puedes verificar si un solo sobre cubre tu área o necesitas comprar más.

---

## Errores comunes al estimar semillas

1. **Confundir densidad de siembra con densidad final de planta.** Se siembra más denso a propósito para compensar germinación fallida; el raleo posterior lleva la densidad al objetivo productivo.
2. **Ignorar el espaciado entre surcos.** La densidad en semillas/m² asume distribución homogénea o surcos a distancia estándar. Si haces surcos más separados, la densidad real baja y sobrarán semillas.
3. **Aplicar el mismo margen a todas las especies.** El rábano germina con >90 % incluso en condiciones caseras; la zanahoria y el perejil son notoriamente irregulares y justifican márgenes del 25–30 %.
4. **No considerar resiembras.** En cultivos de ciclo corto como rábano o baby-leaf, muchos huertos hacen 3–4 siembras escalonadas (cada 2–3 semanas) para cosecha continua. Multiplica la cantidad calculada por el número de rondas previstas.

---

## Qué NO calcula esta herramienta

- **Profundidad de siembra** ni condiciones de suelo específicas.
- **Rendimiento esperado en peso o volumen** — para eso se necesita conocer el marco de plantación definitivo y las condiciones de cultivo.
- **Semillas para propagación vegetativa** (bulbos, estolones, esquejes).
- **Ajustes por siembra en bandejas con sustrato comercial**, donde la germinación suele ser más alta (85–95 %) que en suelo directo.

faq.q: How many seeds per square meter for carrots?
faq.a: Sow **200 carrot seeds per square meter** for direct sowing, then thin to 80–100 mature plants/m² (roughly 5 × 2 cm spacing). Carrot seeds are tiny (≈ 0.8 mg each), so a standard 5 g packet contains 3,500–5,000 seeds — enough for 17–25 m². Use the calculator above to get the exact count for your patch size.

faq.q: How many seeds per square meter for lettuce?
faq.a: Sow **60 lettuce seeds per square meter** for head varieties, thinning to 16–25 final plants/m² at 25–30 cm spacing. For baby-leaf (cut-and-come-again) production, increase to 80–100 seeds/m². Lettuce has around 800–1,000 seeds per gram, so even a small 1 g packet covers 13–16 m².

faq.q: How many seeds per square meter for spinach?
faq.a: Sow **100 spinach seeds per square meter**, thinning to 60–80 plants/m² at 8 × 10 cm. Spinach has one of the lowest germination rates of common vegetables (60–70 %), so sowing at 100/m² compensates and gives you enough to thin. A standard 10 g packet (≈ 800–1,000 seeds) covers 8–10 m².

faq.q: How many seeds per square meter for radishes?
faq.a: Sow **110 radish seeds per square meter**, thinning to 80–100 plants/m² at 5 × 5 cm. Radishes germinate fast (3–5 days) and have an 80–90 % germination rate, so losses are low. A 5 g packet (≈ 400–600 seeds) covers roughly 4–5 m².

faq.q: How many seeds per square meter for tomatoes?
faq.a: Tomatoes are almost always started in seedling trays rather than direct-sown. Use **10 seeds per square meter of tray area**, sowing 2 seeds per cell and thinning to the strongest. The final planting density in the garden bed is **3–4 tomato plants per square meter** (50–70 cm spacing). One standard 0.2 g packet (≈ 60–70 seeds) is enough for 6–7 m² of tray.

faq.q: Should I direct-sow or start transplants indoors?
faq.a: **Direct sow**: crops that dislike root disturbance — carrots, radishes, spinach, beets, parsnips. Sow seeds straight into the final bed. **Start indoors as transplants**: warm-season crops (tomatoes, peppers, eggplants) that need a long growing season. Start 6–8 weeks before last frost, then transplant when soil temperature exceeds 15°C. **Either method works**: lettuce, kale, chard — direct sowing is cheaper; transplants give a 4–6 week head start.

faq.q: How do I test whether my old seeds are still viable?
faq.a: Place 10 seeds on a damp paper towel, fold, seal in a plastic bag and leave at room temperature for 7–10 days. Count how many germinate. If 8 of 10 sprout, you have 80% viability and the standard sowing density is fine. If only 5 sprout (50%), sow 2× the normal density. Expected viability by age (cool dry storage): lettuce/tomato/radish 4–6 years; spinach/beet/peas 3–4 years; carrot/parsley 1–3 years; onion 1–2 years.

faq.q: What planting depth is correct for each crop?
faq.a: General rule: plant seeds at 2–3× their own diameter. **Carrot**: 0.5–1 cm (tiny seeds — barely cover with fine soil). **Radish**: 1–2 cm. **Spinach**: 1.5–2 cm. **Lettuce**: 0.5 cm or press onto surface. **Tomato** (tray): 0.5–1 cm. Planting too deep is the #1 cause of poor germination in small-seeded crops — the seedling runs out of energy before reaching light.

faq.q: Can I apply these seed densities to raised beds and containers?
faq.a: Yes — the seeds-per-square-meter figures apply equally to raised beds, in-ground plots and large containers. The planting area is what matters, not the structure around it. For containers smaller than 0.5 m² (e.g. a 30 × 30 cm pot), just scale down: 0.09 m² × 200 seeds/m² = 18 carrot seeds in that pot. Square-foot gardening grids translate directly — 1 square foot ≈ 0.093 m².

faq.q: How long will unused seeds stay viable?
faq.a: Stored in a cool (5–15°C), dry, dark place: lettuce, tomato, radish, brassicas = 4–6 years; spinach, beet, peas, beans = 3–4 years; carrot, parsley, parsnip = 1–3 years; onion, leek, sweet corn = 1–2 years. Sealed in an airtight container with a silica-gel packet in a refrigerator, viability extends further. Always label packets with species, variety and harvest or purchase year.
